the first assisted migration program in Canada has been successfully developed by changing the scientific discourses associated with best forest practices, from an ecological discourse that emphasizes the preservation of historical species assemblages and mimicking natural disturbances to a genetic discourse that emphasizes the genetic diversity of species and the use of genetic engineering to enhance species’ resilience to climate change.

the assisted migration policy for larch in British Colombia was developed in a way that avoided controversy in the scientific community, which is a signal of institutional change at the level of policy ideas and discourses oriented externally in the policy development process.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the assisted migration of species in Canada will likely be implemented through the development of assisted migration policies that rely on a genetics discourse to avoid the controversy of the idea in the ecological and conservation communities.

the institutional change that is occurring in forestry in Canada is not necessarily a result of the scientific community, but rather of a shift in the discourse that is occurring in the forest industry and in the policy community, which is in turn influencing scientific research.

institutional change in forestry can be observed through changes in discourses in the policy process and the policy ideas they support, and that this institutional change may not be driven by science, but rather by the political context in which science is deployed.
